issue_context.title: Obsolete BindingAddress ctor
issue_context.body:
BindingAddress is read only and has a Parse method. The default constructor wasn't made private so you can create a BindingAddress, but can't do anything with it.

Should obsolete and then remove.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.http.bindingaddress?view=aspnetcore-5.0
comments:
Searched in chem and couldn't find usages.

Discussed in servers team and decided not to create an announcement for this. There is no reason to call this ctor.

review_comments:
Nit:

```suggestion
            var requestLineLength = _methodText!.Length + _scheme.Length + hostText.Length + path.Length;
```

Really, all references to `Scheme` in this method should probably be to `_scheme`. This looks like a similar mistake to the one that was made in HttpProtocol.ProduceContinue where it references RequestHeaders instead of HttpRequestHeaders.

We should come up with a convention to make it clear with properties are user-settable and which ones are the internal representation. This isn't a huge deal though. For a lot of properties we don't have separate user-settable and internal representations.
_scheme is private. If this will change then it should happen in another PR.
Can we make this non-nullable.
It is set to null in HTTP/2
I'd prefer if the feature didn't work at all in HTTP/2

You think there should never be a min request data rate for HTTP/2? Or you think there shouldn't be a way to disable it for HTTP/2?

You should create a new issue. Right now this property definitely supports being set to null. gRPC does it for streaming.

I think the feature should either exist and work or not exist. Right now the feature is on and we don't support it for HTTP/2. 

This feature solely exists for that property so its strange that the feature is returned then the property is null

It does exist.

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/28050#discussion_r530711619

Do we know that option.IPEndPoint isn't null here @jkotalik? Now that IMultiplexedConnectionListenerFactory is experimentally public, I figure it's theoretically possible. I might just add a null check on option.IPEndPoint in the above if condition.
I'm going to leave this as it. This is experimental, and at the moment I think an exception to say that something is wrong is preferable to silently doing the wrong thing.
The TestServiceContext sets all of these except for Heartbeat in its ctor. We could add the ctor but keep the setters.
Meh, the only reason I've been adding constructors is because properties + nullable doesn't work well. Since everything here is forced to have a value then it doesn't matter.

If we don't end up making these non-nullable, we should handle the case where it becomes null between the timeout triggering and the handler actually running. I agree with @davidfowl we should make this non-nullable and just remove the feature for HTTP/2 until if/when we implement it.

I'm confused what you and David are asking for. It is implemented today. I can be set to null today:

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/f98959f630f916d74ccdb705bd02ab34b86fcf85/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Features/IHttpMinRequestBodyDataRateFeature.cs#L17

gRPC has used it since .NET Core 3

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet/blob/ef77760676ce19c279d5480bca68af3ea4d60e96/src/Grpc.AspNetCore.Server/Internal/CallHandlers/ServerCallHandlerBase.cs#L109-L113

I completely forgot about that! We have to keep it nullable then. As unlikely as it is, we should just do the guard against the case where it becomes null between the timeout triggering and the handler actually running.

Its a little weird that TContext has generic constraint of notnull, but the only place it is used is nullable.

Is notnull a way of saying "this type can be anything but `Nullable<Struct>`"

I think this is the way it is because if flows from `IHttpApplication<TContext>` which has the same constraint. You can use your own implementation of that if you call IServer.StartAsync directly, and we probably don't want to have to reason about `IHttpApplication<HttpContext?>` and the like.
I'm surprised the compiler needed the help given the above line.

This seems to only be used to log, and the log only contains this message. If this really can be null, we should probably fix the log message to at least tell us something when CheckCertificateStateResult.Message is null.

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/f98959f630f916d74ccdb705bd02ab34b86fcf85/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/LoggerExtensions.cs#L43-L47

I can only be null when result is false.

I've renamed the properties on this type. Result -> Success, Message -> FailureMesssage. Makes what is going on more obvious.
Are there any tests with a PEM file that doesn't have a private key?
A private key is required to function.
I know. At the moment I think that no private key will NRE instead of giving a useful error message.

@javiercn 

We should probably throw a useful error and add a test for this.
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/28172
Any particular reason for not including both of these above properties in the context ctor?
I made values that are settable as properties only.
